claim: Several universal genomic traits affect trade-offs in the capacity, cost, and efficiency of the biochemical information processing that underpins metabolism and reproduction.
source: Several universal genomic traits affect trade-offs in the capacity, cost, and efficiency of the biochemical information processing that underpins metabolism and reproduction.
evidence: This is a foundational claim stated in the abstract, drawing on established scientific understanding of genomic traits and their functional roles.

claim: Mean bacterial genome size was higher in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: Consistent with predictions, the mean estimated genome size of bacteria was 25% higher in the fertilized treatment (p=0.011), with nutrient enrichment explaining 75% of the variation between samples in mean genome size (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 25% increase with p=0.011 and R2=75%, and visualized in Figure 1B.

claim: GC content of open reading frames was higher in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: The GC content of open reading frames of DNA was 9.9% higher in the fertilized treatment: 54% compared to 49% in the unfertilized treatment (p=0.007, R2 = 86%).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 9.9% increase with p=0.007 and R2=86%.

claim: The per sequence occurrence rate of tRNA genes was higher in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: The per sequence occurrence rate of tRNA genes and the total number of tRNA genes per community were 93% and 64% higher, respectively, in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment (p<0.001 and p=0.065 with R2 = 53%, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 93% increase with p<0.001.

claim: The total number of tRNA genes per community was higher in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: The per sequence occurrence rate of tRNA genes and the total number of tRNA genes per community were 93% and 64% higher, respectively, in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment (p<0.001 and p=0.065 with R2 = 53%, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 64% increase with p=0.065 and R2=53%, and visualized in Figure 1C.

claim: The per sequence occurrence rate of 16S rRNA genes was higher in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: Likewise, in the fertilized treatment, the per sequence occurrence rate of 16S rRNA genes and total number of rRNA operons per community were 119% and 86% higher, respectively (p<0.001 and p=0.096 with R2 = 50%, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 119% increase with p<0.001.

claim: The total number of rRNA operons per community was higher in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: Likewise, in the fertilized treatment, the per sequence occurrence rate of 16S rRNA genes and total number of rRNA operons per community were 119% and 86% higher, respectively (p<0.001 and p=0.096 with R2 = 50%, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 86% increase with p=0.096 and R2=50%, and visualized in Figure 1D.

claim: Codon usage bias in ribosomal protein sequences was higher in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: Consistent with predictions, nutrient enrichment also increased codon usage bias in ribosomal protein genes according to two measures of codon usage bias—the effective number of codons (ENC) and ENC′ (Figure 1E and Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing decreased ENC (6.7% decrease, p=0.018, R2=66%) and ENC′ (4.8% decrease, p=0.031, R2=55%), which indicates increased codon usage bias, and visualized in Figures 1E and 2.

claim: Biomass increased substantially in response to nutrient enrichment.
source: Biomass and chlorophyll a concentrations increased substantially in response to nutrient enrichment (biomass—198% mean increase, p=0.009; chlorophyll a—831% mean increase, p=0.001; Appendix 1—figure 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 198% increase with p=0.009, referenced in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: Chlorophyll a concentrations increased substantially in response to nutrient enrichment.
source: Biomass and chlorophyll a concentrations increased substantially in response to nutrient enrichment (biomass—198% mean increase, p=0.009; chlorophyll a—831% mean increase, p=0.001; Appendix 1—figure 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 831% increase with p=0.001, referenced in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The ratio of phosphorus to carbon (P:C) in seston biomass increased in response to nutrient enrichment.
source: as did the ratio of phosphorus to carbon (P:C) in seston biomass (19.5% mean increase, p=0.014, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 19.5% increase with p=0.014, and visualized in Figure 1A.

claim: The percentages of bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya, and viruses making up the community were not discernibly different between unfertilized and fertilized treatments.
source: As the percentages of bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya, and viruses making up the community were not discernibly different between unfertilized and fertilized treatments (p=0.46, 0.37, 0.39, 0.21, respectively)
evidence: Supported by statistical tests showing no significant differences (p>0.05 for all groups).

claim: Bacteria made up 94% of the metagenomes.
source: these genomic changes reflected changes in the abundances of taxa at finer phylogenetic scales, in particular of bacterial taxa, which made up 94% of the metagenomes
evidence: Supported by metagenomic composition data.

claim: 188 genera showed changes in abundance with p<0.05.
source: Furthermore, the genomic changes reflected widespread changes within the community—they were not driven by just a few specific populations, as 188 genera showed changes in abundance (with p<0.05) and no single genus dominated the community (the highest relative abundance of a taxon at the genus level was 4%).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of taxonomic abundance changes.

claim: No single genus dominated the community, with the highest relative abundance of a taxon at the genus level being 4%.
source: Furthermore, the genomic changes reflected widespread changes within the community—they were not driven by just a few specific populations, as 188 genera showed changes in abundance (with p<0.05) and no single genus dominated the community (the highest relative abundance of a taxon at the genus level was 4%).
evidence: Supported by metagenomic taxonomic composition data.

claim: Nutrient enrichment explained 86% of the variation in community genomic trait composition along a single principal component axis.
source: The single PCA axis captured 78% of the variance in the genomic traits for the communities, and nutrient treatment explained 86% of the variation in community genomic trait composition along this single axis of trophic strategy (general linear model [GLM]–p=0.004; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by PCA and GLM analysis showing R2=86% with p=0.004, and visualized in Figure 3.

claim: Oligotrophy favors lower information-processing costs whereas copiotrophy favors higher processing rates.
source: as predicted on the basis of the assumption that oligotrophy favors lower information-processing costs whereas copiotrophy favors higher processing rates.
evidence: This is stated as the theoretical basis for the predictions in the abstract.

claim: Organisms must be able to store, copy, and translate the information contained in genetic material.
source: Organisms must be able to store, copy, and translate the information contained in genetic material.
evidence: This is a statement of fundamental biological knowledge about cellular information processing.

claim: Organisms must be able to update their transcriptome and proteome adaptively in response to altered environmental conditions.
source: And, they must be able to update their transcriptome and proteome adaptively in response to altered environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a statement of fundamental biological knowledge about cellular adaptation.

claim: For an organism to grow and reproduce rapidly, rates at every step of the metabolic network must be sufficiently high such that no single step is unduly rate-limiting, including the information processes that underpin biosynthesis and regulate metabolic networks.
source: For an organism to grow and reproduce rapidly, rates at every step of the metabolic network must be sufficiently high such that no single step is unduly rate-limiting, including the information processes that underpin biosynthesis and regulate metabolic networks.
evidence: This is a statement based on established principles of metabolic control and systems biology.

claim: The structure and size of the genome affect the rate, efficiency, and robustness of the information processes that support metabolism, growth, and reproduction.
source: The structure and size of the genome affect the rate, efficiency, and robustness of the information processes that support metabolism, growth, and reproduction (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with reference to Appendix 1 for further details.

claim: There are necessary tradeoffs in the costs and benefits of genomic features.
source: There are necessary tradeoffs in the costs and benefits of these features (Appendix 1; see also Smith, 1976)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith, 1976 and reference to Appendix 1.

claim: Tradeoffs in genomic features should make individual organisms more competitive in and better-suited to only particular ranges of growth and trophic conditions.
source: which should consequently make individual organisms more competitive in and better-suited to only particular ranges of growth and trophic conditions (Roller and Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on tradeoff theory, supported by citation to Roller and Schmidt, 2015.

claim: Copiotrophs must have the capacity for intracellular rates of information processing that are sufficiently high to support high rates of metabolism and reproduction.
source: Organisms that are best suited to compete in environments where resources are abundant (copiotrophs) must have the capacity for intracellular rates of information processing that are sufficiently high to support high rates of metabolism and reproduction.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for copiotrophic organisms based on their ecological strategy.

claim: Maintaining the genomic and structural capacity for rapid growth is costly, potentially placing copiotrophic taxa at a disadvantage in stable, nutrient-poor environments where growth rates are chronically slow.
source: However, maintaining the genomic and structural capacity for rapid growth is costly, potentially placing copiotrophic taxa at a disadvantage in stable, nutrient-poor environments where growth rates are chronically slow (Giovannoni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about ecological tradeoffs, supported by citation to Giovannoni et al., 2014.

claim: Oligotrophic environments may favor organisms which have information processing machinery that is less costly to build, maintain, and operate, thereby increasing resource use efficiency and growth efficiency.
source: Oligotrophic environments may thus instead favor organisms (oligotrophs), which have information processing machinery that is less costly to build, maintain, and operate, thereby increasing resource use efficiency and growth efficiency (Koch, 2001; Roller and Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about oligotrophic adaptation, supported by citations to Koch, 2001 and Roller and Schmidt, 2015.

claim: Genomic traits that affect the rates and costs of biochemical information processing within cells can influence the degree to which an organism is optimized for oligotrophy versus copiotrophy.
source: Genomic traits that affect the rates and costs of biochemical information processing within cells can thus influence the degree to which an organism is optimized for oligotrophy versus copiotrophy.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the preceding discussion of tradeoffs and ecological strategies.

claim: The oligotrophic-copiotrophic strategy continuum is reminiscent of the classic slow-fast life history continuum.
source: This oligotrophic-copiotrophic strategy continuum is reminiscent of the classic slow-fast life history continuum (Stearns, 1992)
evidence: This is a comparison to established ecological theory, supported by citation to Stearns, 1992.

claim: The oligotrophic-copiotrophic strategy continuum is reminiscent of classical r/K selection theory.
source: This oligotrophic-copiotrophic strategy continuum is reminiscent of the classic slow-fast life history continuum (Stearns, 1992), of classical r/K selection theory (MacArthur and Wilson, 2001; Pianka, 1972; Pianka, 1970)
evidence: This is a comparison to established ecological theory, supported by citations to MacArthur and Wilson, 2001; Pianka, 1972; Pianka, 1970.

claim: Traits associated with biological rates and efficiencies of resource use, growth, and reproduction play an important role in community assembly.
source: In conjunction with research on the role of functional traits and niches in shaping the assembly of communities (e.g., Fukami et al., 2005; Litchman and Klausmeier, 2008; McGill et al., 2006; Okie and Brown, 2009; Roller and Schmidt, 2015), this work suggests that traits that are associated with the biological rates and efficiencies of resource use, growth, and reproduction play an important role in community assembly.
evidence: This is an inference from cited research on functional traits and community assembly.

claim: It is unclear whether traits specifically related to rates and costs of biochemical information processing have sufficiently pronounced tradeoffs or physiological effects to play an important role in the evolutionary ecology of organisms and in the assembly of communities.
source: It is unclear, however, whether the traits that are specifically related to rates and costs of biochemical information processing have sufficiently pronounced tradeoffs or physiological effects to play an important role in the evolutionary ecology of organisms and in the assembly of communities, although there are some promising indications (Dethlefsen, 2004; Roller et al., 2016).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the literature, with citations to some promising work.

claim: Relatively few studies have coupled metagenomics with a trait-based framework to clarify the drivers of community assembly.
source: To date, relatively few studies have coupled metagenomics with a trait-based framework to clarify the drivers of community assembly (Burke et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2008; Mackelprang et al., 2011; Raes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: No studies have deployed metagenomic and trait-based approaches in the context of whole-ecosystem experimentation to test ecologically relevant hypotheses under field conditions.
source: Even fewer (indeed, none that we are aware of) have deployed such approaches in the context of whole-ecosystem experimentation to test ecologically relevant hypotheses under field conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Research on genomic traits has revealed correlations of these traits with growth and trophic strategy in a variety of eukaryotic and prokaryotic species.
source: Research on the genomic traits described above has revealed correlations of these traits with growth and trophic strategy in a variety of eukaryotic and prokaryotic species (Vieira-Silva and Rocha, 2010)
evidence: This is a summary of prior research findings, supported by citation to Vieira-Silva and Rocha, 2010.

claim: Research has started to unravel the mechanisms by which genomic traits influence fitness.
source: and started to unravel the mechanisms by which these traits influence fitness (Appendix 1), suggesting that they may play an important role in ecology (Freilich et al., 2009; Lauro et al., 2009; Weider et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a summary of prior research findings, supported by citations and reference to Appendix 1.

claim: Work published to date has tended to look at only one or two genomic traits at a time.
source: However, the work published to date has tended to look at only one or two of these traits at a time (Zeigler Allen et al., 2012; Raes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: More work is required to help resolve incongruities in the literature regarding the evolutionary ecology of bacteria genome size.
source: More work is also required to help resolve incongruities in the literature, such as different views on the evolutionary ecology of bacteria genome size (e.g., DeLong et al., 2010 versus Vieira-Silva and Rocha, 2010) (Appendix 1).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature, citing conflicting studies.

claim: Most ecological studies of genomic traits have been based on studies of microbial isolates, comparative analyses, or sampling across environmental gradients.
source: Importantly, most ecological studies of these traits have been based on studies of microbial isolates, comparative analyses, or sampling across environmental gradients (Zeigler Allen et al., 2012; Foerstner et al., 2005; Freilich et al., 2009; Raes et al., 2007; Roller et al., 2013; Vieira-Silva and Rocha, 2010).
evidence: This is a characterization of the methodological approaches in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Experimental work examining the role of genomic traits in mediating the structure of communities under natural conditions is extremely limited.
source: Experimental work examining their role in mediating the structure of communities under natural conditions is extremely limited.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Most microbial taxa are uncultivable in isolation.
source: Given (1) the complexity of the biotic and abiotic interactions that shape communities, (2) that most microbial taxa are uncultivable in isolation (Ho et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a statement of established microbiological knowledge, supported by citation to Ho et al., 2017.

claim: Community traits can have widely different responses to temporal/experimental versus geographic variation in abiotic variables.
source: and (3) that community traits can have widely different responses to temporal/experimental versus geographic variation in abiotic variables (e.g., Sandel et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a statement about ecological patterns, supported by citation to Sandel et al., 2010.

claim: Direct experimentation in the field with complex communities is required to better establish the validity of inferences about molecular adaptations for ecological dynamics in nature.
source: direct experimentation in the field with complex communities is required to better establish the validity of inferences about these purported molecular adaptations for ecological dynamics in nature.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the need for field experiments based on the limitations of other approaches.

claim: Lagunita is an oligotrophic, highly phosphorus-deficient pond in Cuatro Ciénegas, Mexico.
source: Our study site is Lagunita, an oligotrophic, highly phosphorus-deficient pond in Cuatro Ciénegas, a biological reserve in Mexico (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the study site, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: This study is one of the first whole-ecosystem experiments to involve experiment-level replicated metagenomic assessments of community response.
source: Our study is noteworthy as one of the first whole-ecosystem experiments to involve experiment-level replicated metagenomic assessments of community response.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study design based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: If individual genomic features affect the ability of organisms to survive and reproduce as a function of nutrient availability, then collective measures of these features at the metagenomic level should exhibit these characteristics and reflect organisms' responses to experimental fertilization.
source: If it is true that individual genomic features do indeed affect the ability of organisms to survive and reproduce as a function of nutrient availability, then collective measures of these features at the metagenomic level (which aggregates the genomes of all of the individuals constituting a community) should likewise exhibit these characteristics and should reflect the organisms' responses to experimental fertilization (Krause et al., 2014; Wallenstein and Hall, 2012).
evidence: This is a logical inference about how individual-level traits should manifest at the community level, supported by citations.

claim: The mean ENC of ribosomal protein sequences decreased with fertilization by 6.7%.
source: The mean ENC and ENC′ of ribosomal protein sequences detected in the metagenomes decreased with fertilization by 6.7% and 4.8%, respectively, indicating increased codon usage bias (ENC: p=0.018, R2 = 66%; ENC′: p=0.031, R2 = 55%).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 6.7% decrease with p=0.018 and R2=66%.

claim: The mean ENC′ of ribosomal protein sequences decreased with fertilization by 4.8%.
source: The mean ENC and ENC′ of ribosomal protein sequences detected in the metagenomes decreased with fertilization by 6.7% and 4.8%, respectively, indicating increased codon usage bias (ENC: p=0.018, R2 = 66%; ENC′: p=0.031, R2 = 55%).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing 4.8% decrease with p=0.031 and R2=55%.

claim: Median ENC was lower in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: Median ENC and ENC′ were also lower in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment (p=0.006, R2 = 75% and p=0.010; R2 = 75%)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with p=0.006 and R2=75%.

claim: Median ENC′ was lower in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment.
source: Median ENC and ENC′ were also lower in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment (p=0.006, R2 = 75% and p=0.010; R2 = 75%)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with p=0.010 and R2=75%.

claim: The distributions of ENC in ribosomal protein sequences significantly differed between treatments.
source: and Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests indicated that the distributions of ENC and ENC′ in ribosomal protein sequences significantly differed between treatments (all p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests with p<0.01.

claim: The distributions of ENC′ in ribosomal protein sequences significantly differed between treatments.
source: and Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests indicated that the distributions of ENC and ENC′ in ribosomal protein sequences significantly differed between treatments (all p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests with p<0.01.

claim: A greater frequency of sequences exhibited little-to-no codon usage bias (ENC and ENC′ values around 60–61) in the unfertilized communities.
source: In particular, as shown in Figure 2A and B, a greater frequency of sequences exhibited little-to-no codon usage bias (ENC and ENC′ values around 60–61) in the unfertilized communities (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by distribution data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: In the fertilized treatment, there were notably higher numbers of ribosomal protein sequences with extremely high codon usage bias (ENC and ENC′ <~37).
source: whereas in the fertilized treatment, there were notably higher numbers of ribosomal protein sequences with extremely high codon usage bias (ENC and ENC′ <~37).
evidence: Supported by distribution data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The variance in the P:C ratio substantially decreased with fertilization by a factor of 8.
source: As suggested by Figures 1 and 2, the variance in the P:C ratio and in the mean and median codon usage bias of communities (quantified by ENC′, the more powerful indicator of codon usage bias) substantially decreased with fertilization by around an order of magnitude or more—by factors of 8, 31, and 27, respectively (P:C ratio–p=0.058; mean ENC′–p=0.056; median ENC′–p=0.069; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.058, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1 and Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The variance in mean codon usage bias (ENC′) substantially decreased with fertilization by a factor of 31.
source: As suggested by Figures 1 and 2, the variance in the P:C ratio and in the mean and median codon usage bias of communities (quantified by ENC′, the more powerful indicator of codon usage bias) substantially decreased with fertilization by around an order of magnitude or more—by factors of 8, 31, and 27, respectively (P:C ratio–p=0.058; mean ENC′–p=0.056; median ENC′–p=0.069; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.056, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1 and Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The variance in median codon usage bias (ENC′) substantially decreased with fertilization by a factor of 27.
source: As suggested by Figures 1 and 2, the variance in the P:C ratio and in the mean and median codon usage bias of communities (quantified by ENC′, the more powerful indicator of codon usage bias) substantially decreased with fertilization by around an order of magnitude or more—by factors of 8, 31, and 27, respectively (P:C ratio–p=0.058; mean ENC′–p=0.056; median ENC′–p=0.069; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.069, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1 and Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Variance in genome size decreased substantially with fertilization by a factor of 10.
source: Variance in genome size and mean and median ENC also decreased substantially by factors of 10, 10, and 6, respectively, but these responses are less certain (genome size–p=0.174; mean ENC–p=0.169; median ENC–p=0.275; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.174, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: Variance in mean ENC decreased substantially with fertilization by a factor of 10.
source: Variance in genome size and mean and median ENC also decreased substantially by factors of 10, 10, and 6, respectively, but these responses are less certain (genome size–p=0.174; mean ENC–p=0.169; median ENC–p=0.275; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.169, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: Variance in median ENC decreased substantially with fertilization by a factor of 6.
source: Variance in genome size and mean and median ENC also decreased substantially by factors of 10, 10, and 6, respectively, but these responses are less certain (genome size–p=0.174; mean ENC–p=0.169; median ENC–p=0.275; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.275, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: Variance in the log-transformed number of tRNA genes substantially increased with fertilization by 846%.
source: By contrast, variance in the log-transformed number of tRNA genes and rRNA operons substantially increased with fertilization, by 846% and 655%, respectively (rRNA–p<0.001; tRNA–p=0.013)
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.013, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: Variance in the log-transformed number of rRNA operons substantially increased with fertilization by 655%.
source: By contrast, variance in the log-transformed number of tRNA genes and rRNA operons substantially increased with fertilization, by 846% and 655%, respectively (rRNA–p<0.001; tRNA–p=0.013)
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p<0.001, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: GC content variance did not exhibit any change with fertilization.
source: whereas GC content variance did not appear to exhibit any change (p=0.56; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis with p=0.56, referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: The single PCA axis captured 78% of the variance in the genomic traits for the communities.
source: The single PCA axis captured 78% of the variance in the genomic traits for the communities, and nutrient treatment explained 86% of the variation in community genomic trait composition along this single axis of trophic strategy (general linear model [GLM]–p=0.004; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis, visualized in Figure 3.

claim: The fertilization study demonstrated strong nutrient limitation in the Lagunita ecosystem.
source: Our fertilization study demonstrated strong nutrient limitation in the Lagunita ecosystem, as manifested by increased biomass, chlorophyll content, and P:C ratios of plankton in the fertilized pond versus the unenriched mesocosms.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results showing increased biomass, chlorophyll, and P:C ratios.

claim: Strong differences in information-processing traits between the fertilized pond and unfertilized internal mesocosms agree with all five directional predictions.
source: Using metagenomics, we found strong differences in information-processing traits between the fertilized pond and unfertilized internal mesocosms, which agree with all five of our directional predictions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results matching predictions.

claim: The observed genomic trait differences result primarily from differences in the growth and nutrient conditions of the two treatments.
source: We thus interpret the observed genomic trait differences as resulting primarily from differences in the growth and nutrient conditions of the two treatments.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental results.

claim: The trait differences primarily reflect trait-mediated ecological dynamics rather than microevolutionary changes within populations.
source: We interpret these differences as primarily reflecting trait-mediated ecological dynamics—the differential success of lineages present within the pond and colonization by other lineages—rather than microevolutionary changes within populations.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on the short experimental timeframe.

claim: The relatively short time period of the experiment (32 days) encompasses a relatively low maximum number of generations of replication, limiting the opportunity for measurable genomic evolution to occur.
source: Our reasoning is that the relatively short time period of our experiment (32 days) encompasses a relatively low maximum number of generations of replication (Appendix 1), and so limited the opportunity for measurable genomic evolution to occur (e.g., Lenski and Travisano, 1994).
evidence: This is reasoning based on the experimental timeframe and citation to evolutionary studies.

claim: Ecologically significant phenotypic information about communities can be uncovered using a read-based metagenomic approach.
source: Overall, our study suggests that ecologically significant phenotypic information about communities can be uncovered using a read-based approach (metagenomics) that leverages the relevant abundance and DNA characteristics of conserved genetic elements.
evidence: This is an inference from the successful application of the metagenomic approach in this study.

claim: The read-based metagenomic approach avoids biases associated with massive gaps in microbial taxonomic databases and cross-taxonomy assembly efficiencies.
source: Importantly, this approach avoids the biases associated with the massive gaps that are present in microbial taxonomic databases and cross-taxonomy assembly efficiencies (Kunin et al., 2010; Sogin et al., 2006; Temperton and Giovannoni, 2012; Yooseph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about methodological advantages, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Nutrient enrichment explained 50% or more of the variation in each genomic trait.
source: Remarkably, nutrient enrichment explained 50% or more of the variation in each trait and 88% of the co-variation of these five traits along a single statistical dimension quantifying the oligotrophy-copiotrophy strategy continuum (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical results, visualized in Figure 3.

claim: Nutrient enrichment explained 88% of the co-variation of the five genomic traits along a single statistical dimension quantifying the oligotrophy-copiotrophy strategy continuum.
source: Remarkably, nutrient enrichment explained 50% or more of the variation in each trait and 88% of the co-variation of these five traits along a single statistical dimension quantifying the oligotrophy-copiotrophy strategy continuum (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the PCA results, visualized in Figure 3.

claim: The congruence of all trait responses with predictions suggests that the effects of genomic traits on the rates and costs of biochemical information-processing are sufficiently pronounced to play a role in community assembly.
source: The congruence of all trait responses with our predictions suggests that the effects of these genomics traits on the rates and costs of biochemical information-processing are sufficiently pronounced to play a role in community assembly.
evidence: This is an inference from the consistency of results with predictions.

claim: The fertilized community had genomic traits expected to augment translational capacity.
source: We found that the fertilized community had genomic traits that were expected to augment translational capacity, whereas the unfertilized communities had genomic traits that lower the costs of biochemical information processing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The unfertilized communities had genomic traits that lower the costs of biochemical information processing.
source: We found that the fertilized community had genomic traits that were expected to augment translational capacity, whereas the unfertilized communities had genomic traits that lower the costs of biochemical information processing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Increased codon usage bias in ribosomal protein genes can improve the speed and accuracy of translation of ribosomal proteins by increasing the rate at which tRNAs bind to mRNA codons.
source: For instance, the fertilized community had increased codon usage bias in ribosomal protein genes, which can improve the speed and accuracy of translation of ribosomal proteins by increasing the rate at which tRNAs bind to mRNA codons of ribosomal protein genes, as well as by possibly reducing the likelihood of mistranslation (Higgs and Ran, 2008; Figures 1E and 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the observed trait change, supported by citation to Higgs and Ran, 2008 and shown in Figures 1E and 2.

claim: Increased codon usage bias may reduce the likelihood of mistranslation.
source: For instance, the fertilized community had increased codon usage bias in ribosomal protein genes, which can improve the speed and accuracy of translation of ribosomal proteins by increasing the rate at which tRNAs bind to mRNA codons of ribosomal protein genes, as well as by possibly reducing the likelihood of mistranslation (Higgs and Ran, 2008; Figures 1E and 2).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism, supported by citation to Higgs and Ran, 2008.

claim: The increase in the rate of production of ribosomes supports larger ribosomal pools undergirding higher overall rates of protein synthesis.
source: The resulting increase in the rate of production of ribosomes supports the larger ribosomal pools undergirding higher overall rates of protein synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequence of increased ribosome production.

claim: The finding of higher numbers of rRNA and tRNA genes in fertilized communities supports the 'Growth Rate Hypothesis'.
source: The fertilized communities also had higher numbers of rRNA and tRNA genes. In conjunction with the observed increase in the biomass P:C ratio, this finding supports the 'Growth Rate Hypothesis'—that fast-growing cells should have higher P-contents that reflect higher concentrations of P-rich ribosomal RNA, which are maintained by increased copies of rRNA and tRNA genes (Elser et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the experimental results to an established hypothesis, supported by citation to Elser et al., 2000.

claim: Fast-growing cells should have higher P-contents that reflect higher concentrations of P-rich ribosomal RNA, which are maintained by increased copies of rRNA and tRNA genes.
source: In conjunction with the observed increase in the biomass P:C ratio, this finding supports the 'Growth Rate Hypothesis'—that fast-growing cells should have higher P-contents that reflect higher concentrations of P-rich ribosomal RNA, which are maintained by increased copies of rRNA and tRNA genes (Elser et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement of the Growth Rate Hypothesis, supported by citation to Elser et al., 2000.

claim: Higher mean genome size in the fertilized pond reflects the need to encode a larger array of genes needed to support expanded translational and catabolic capacity of faster growing cells.
source: Mean genome size was also higher in the fertilized pond, reflecting the need to encode a larger array of genes that are needed to support the expanded translational and catabolic capacity of faster growing cells, and possibly also reflecting the benefits of maintaining a streamlined genome that requires minimal resources for maintenance and replication in nutrient-poor conditions (e.g., Giovannoni et al., 2005; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the genome size difference, supported by citation and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Higher mean genome size in the fertilized pond possibly reflects the benefits of maintaining a streamlined genome that requires minimal resources for maintenance and replication in nutrient-poor conditions.
source: Mean genome size was also higher in the fertilized pond, reflecting the need to encode a larger array of genes that are needed to support the expanded translational and catabolic capacity of faster growing cells, and possibly also reflecting the benefits of maintaining a streamlined genome that requires minimal resources for maintenance and replication in nutrient-poor conditions (e.g., Giovannoni et al., 2005; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about genome streamlining in oligotrophs, supported by citation to Giovannoni et al., 2005.

claim: Low GC-content in oligotrophic taxa is a valuable resource conservation strategy.
source: Consistent with our prediction that low GC-content in oligotrophic taxa is a valuable resource conservation strategy, GC content was lower in the unfertilized communities (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the GC content difference, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Vieira-Silva and Rocha (2010) found no significant interspecific correlation of GC content and genome size with generation time in a comparative study of bacteria.
source: These results contrast with those of Vieira-Silva and Rocha (2010), who found no significant interspecific correlation of GC content and genome size with generation time in a comparative study of bacteria (Vieira-Silva et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: The difference in results between this study and Vieira-Silva and Rocha (2010) may reflect confounding variables and pronounced statistical error inherent to interspecific microbial growth and trait databases.
source: The difference in results may reflect multiple factors, including: (1) the presence of confounding variables and pronounced statistical error (measurement and biological) inherent to interspecific microbial growth and trait databases that are collated from a variety of sources (e.g., ecosystems, conditions such as temperature), as in their study;
evidence: This is speculation about reasons for different results.

claim: The difference in results may reflect an underrepresentation in databases of unculturable prokaryotic species that may comprise the majority of species in microbiomes and which typically have different evolutionary ecologies than culturable taxa.
source: (2) an underrepresentation in databases of the unculturable prokaryotic species that may comprise the majority of species in microbiomes, such as Lagunitas, and which typically have different evolutionary ecologies than culturable taxa (Pande and Kost, 2017; Swan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about reasons for different results, supported by citations to Pande and Kost, 2017 and Swan et al., 2013.

claim: The findings are largely consistent with observational studies of metagenomes and genomes along productivity gradients, and with comparisons across species varying in growth rate.
source: Overall, however, our findings are largely consistent with observational studies of metagenomes and genomes along productivity gradients, and with comparisons across species varying in growth rate (Zeigler Allen et al., 2012; DeLong et al., 2010; Foerstner et al., 2005; Lauro et al., 2009; Raes et al., 2007; Roller et al., 2013; Swan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Much of the variation in genomic traits along productivity gradients or across species may be attributed to effects of information-processing costs and rates on an oligotrophy-copiotrophy strategy continuum and related adaptive strategies.
source: Our experiment on communities in situ suggests that much of the variation in these genomic traits along productivity gradients or across species may similarly be attributed to effects of information-processing costs and rates on an oligotrophy-copiotrophy strategy continuum and related adaptive strategies, such as r/K selection and Grime's 'C-S-R Triangle' (e.g., Grime and Pierce, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results to broader ecological patterns, with citation to Grime and Pierce, 2012.

claim: The direction of variance changes in response to enrichment differed among the traits.
source: The direction of the changes that occur in response to enrichment differed among the traits, so the variance responses do not simply reflect potential for increased dispersal limitation in unfertilized mesocosms as compared to enriched pond samples (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The variance responses suggest that the strength of a trait's role in filtering the community differs between unenriched and enriched treatments.
source: Instead, all-else-being equal, the responses suggest that the strength of a trait's role in filtering the community differs between unenriched and enriched treatments, which could reflect differences in the degree to which a trait affects the costs versus the rates of information processing.
evidence: This is an inference from the variance patterns observed in the data.

claim: Traits that have more impact on the costs of information processing should play more of a role in oligotrophic environments, whereas traits that have more impact on the rates of information processing should play more of a role in copiotrophic environments.
source: In general, traits that have much more of an impact on the costs of information processing should play more of a role in oligotrophic environments, whereas traits that have more of an impact on the rates of information processing (e.g., probably codon usage bias) should play more of a role in copiotrophic environments.
evidence: This is a general inference about trait-environment relationships.

claim: The substantial reduction in variance levels in codon usage bias in response to fertilization agrees with the viewpoint that evolution of low codon usage bias primarily reflects relaxed selection rather than positive selection for neutral codon usage.
source: The substantial reduction in variance levels in codon usage bias in response to fertilization are in agreement with this viewpoint: the evolution of low codon usage bias is primarily thought to reflect relaxed selection rather than positive selection for neutral (random) codon usage, although many complex issues remain to be resolved (Hershberg and Petrov, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the variance results in light of evolutionary theory, supported by citation to Hershberg and Petrov, 2008.

claim: The highly increased variance in rRNA operon and tRNA gene numbers in response to fertilization may indicate that the augmented P and N requirements of taxa with high rRNA and tRNA gene copy numbers are particularly detrimental in oligotrophic conditions.
source: By contrast, the highly increased variance in rRNA operon and tRNA gene numbers in response to fertilization may indicate that the augmented P and N requirements of taxa that have high rRNA and tRNA gene copy numbers, which tend to have larger pools of ribosomes and other translation machinery, are particularly detrimental in oligotrophic conditions (Stevenson and Schmidt, 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the variance results, supported by citation to Stevenson and Schmidt, 2004.

claim: In nutrient-rich conditions, some organisms may do well even with fairly low numbers of rRNA and tRNA genes, for example by having multiple genome copies or other mechanisms that increase the concentrations and kinetics of RNA polymerase, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, rRNA and tRNA.
source: In nutrient-rich conditions, on the other hand, some organisms may still do well even with fairly low numbers of these genes, for example by having multiple genome copies (e.g., Mendell et al., 2008) or other mechanisms that increase the concentrations and kinetics of RNA polymerase, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, rRNA and tRNA (e.g., Yadavalli and Ibba, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms, supported by citations to Mendell et al., 2008 and Yadavalli and Ibba, 2012.

claim: A 10-fold decrease in variance of mean genome size was observed in the unfertilized mesocosms, implying that genome size has a more variable ecological role in oligotrophic ecosystems.
source: We also observed a 10-fold decrease in variance of mean genome size in the unfertilized mesocosms, implying that genome size has a more variable ecological role in oligotrophic ecosystems, although this change was only suggestive (p=0.17).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an interpretation, noting statistical uncertainty.

claim: Based on genome streamlining theory alone, we would expect reduced variance in genome size in oligotrophic environments.
source: On the basis of genome streamlining theory alone, which suggests that small genomes should be favored in oligotrophic conditions because of the favoring of cellular architectures that minimize resource requirements (Giovannoni et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2012), we would expect reduced variance in genome size in oligotrophic environments, in contradiction with our results.
evidence: This is a statement of theoretical expectation based on cited literature.

claim: There is presumably an interspecific increase in active mass-specific metabolic rate and rmax with genome size in bacteria.
source: There is presumably an interspecific increase in active mass-specific metabolic rate and rmax with genome size in bacteria (DeLong et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a statement of a presumed relationship, supported by citation to DeLong et al., 2010.

claim: Under abruptly enriched conditions, community members with larger genomes may displace the complex and diverse original community by growing faster.
source: so under abruptly enriched conditions, community members that have larger genomes may displace the complex and diverse original community by growing faster.
evidence: This is speculation about community dynamics based on metabolic scaling.

claim: The effects of genome size on metabolic costs may be insufficient to play as strong a role in the evolutionary ecology and assembly of oligotrophic communities.
source: By contrast, it appears that the effects of genome size on metabolic costs may be insufficient to play as strong a role in the evolutionary ecology and assembly of these oligotrophic communities.
evidence: This is an inference from the variance results.

claim: The elemental costs of DNA play a negligible role in the evolutionary ecology of genome size.
source: This suggestion agrees with others who have argued that the elemental costs of DNA play a negligible role in the evolutionary ecology of genome size (Lynch, 2006; Mira et al., 2001; Sterner and Elser, 2002; Vieira-Silva et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a statement of agreement with cited literature.

claim: The smaller genomes found in many parasites, symbionts, and oligotrophs may reflect the mutational loss of genes as the result of relaxed positive selection for keeping non-essential genes.
source: the smaller genomes found in many parasites, symbionts, and oligotrophs may instead reflect the mutational loss of genes as the result of relaxed positive selection for keeping non-essential genes (Mira et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of an alternative explanation for small genomes, supported by citation to Mira et al., 2001.

claim: No change in variance of GC content was observed between treatments.
source: Unlike the other information-processing traits, we observed no change in variance of GC content between treatments.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: It is less clear why there may be filtering for high GC content in response to nutrient enrichment.
source: Although we expected environmental filtering for low GC content in oligotrophic conditions, it is less clear why there may be filtering for high GC content in response to nutrient enrichment, pointing to a need for further investigations into the implications of GC content for microbial physiological and community ecology.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap and need for future research.

claim: All genomic traits studied responded as predicted to nutrient enrichment.
source: The genomic traits studied here affect the costs and rates of biochemical information processing within cells, and all of these traits responded as predicted to nutrient enrichment.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results.

claim: Cells proliferating under nutrient-enriched conditions had increased capacities for transforming and storing information.
source: Cells proliferating under nutrient-enriched conditions had increased capacities for transforming and storing information, whereas those persisting in oligotrophic conditions had genomic traits associated with reduced costs for the information processes that underpin metabolism and reproduction.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Cells persisting in oligotrophic conditions had genomic traits associated with reduced costs for the information processes that underpin metabolism and reproduction.
source: Cells proliferating under nutrient-enriched conditions had increased capacities for transforming and storing information, whereas those persisting in oligotrophic conditions had genomic traits associated with reduced costs for the information processes that underpin metabolism and reproduction.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Optimizing tradeoffs in the efficiency and capacity of information processing may play a vital role in the evolutionary specialization of a microbe's cellular biology to the particular trophic conditions of an ecosystem.
source: Optimizing tradeoffs in the efficiency and capacity of information processing may thus play a vital role in the evolutionary specialization of a microbe's cellular biology to the particular trophic conditions of an ecosystem.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results about evolutionary adaptation.

claim: Information processing traits should be included in the development of trait-based theories and frameworks for microbial community ecology.
source: Information processing traits should be included in the development of trait-based theories and frameworks for microbial community ecology, as apparently all three core components of metabolism—information, energy, and material requirements and transformations—must be closely fine-tuned to the growth and trophic strategy of a microorganism.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: All three core components of metabolism—information, energy, and material requirements and transformations—must be closely fine-tuned to the growth and trophic strategy of a microorganism.
source: as apparently all three core components of metabolism—information, energy, and material requirements and transformations—must be closely fine-tuned to the growth and trophic strategy of a microorganism.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings about metabolic integration.

claim: Lagunita is a shallow pond averaging 35,000 L in volume and roughly 12 m x 4 m.
source: The whole-ecosystem fertilization experiment took place in Lagunita, a shallow (<0.33 m) pond averaging 35,000 L in volume and roughly ~12 m x 4 m.
evidence: This is a description of the study site.

claim: Lagunita is adjacent to a larger lagoon (Laguna Intermedia from the Churince system) in the Cuatro Ciénegas basin.
source: It is adjacent to a larger lagoon (Laguna Intermedia from the Churince system) in the Cuatro Ciénegas basin (CCB), an enclosed evaporitic valley in the Chihuahuan desert, Mexico.
evidence: This is a description of the study site location.

claim: The Cuatro Ciénegas basin is an enclosed evaporitic valley in the Chihuahuan desert, Mexico.
source: It is adjacent to a larger lagoon (Laguna Intermedia from the Churince system) in the Cuatro Ciénegas basin (CCB), an enclosed evaporitic valley in the Chihuahuan desert, Mexico.
evidence: This is a description of the geographic setting.

claim: The Cuatro Ciénegas basin harbors a variety of groundwater-fed springs, streams, and pools.
source: Despite its aridity, the CCB harbors a variety of groundwater-fed springs, streams, and pools.
evidence: This is a description of the study region.

claim: Aquatic environments in the Cuatro Ciénegas basin harbor a high diversity of unique microbiota.
source: Past research has also shown that these aquatic environments harbor a high diversity of unique microbiota (Souza et al., 2018; Souza et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a statement about prior research findings, supported by citations to Souza et al., 2018 and Souza et al., 2006.

claim: Microbiota in the Cuatro Ciénegas basin have evolved under strong stoichiometric imbalance (high nitrogen:phosphorus ratios) and prevalent ecosystem P limitation.
source: which have evolved under strong stoichiometric imbalance (high nitrogen (N):phosphorus (P) ratios) and prevalent ecosystem P limitation (Corman et al., 2016; Elser et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary context, supported by citations to Corman et al., 2016 and Elser et al., 2005.

claim: Lagunita water is high in conductivity, dominated by Ca2+, SO42–, and CO32–.
source: Lagunita water is high in conductivity, dominated by Ca2+, SO42–, and CO32–
evidence: This is a description of water chemistry at the study site.

claim: Lagunita has an average molar TN:TP ratio of 122 indicative of strong P limitation.
source: and has an average molar TN:TP ratio of 122 indicative of strong P limitation, as previously demonstrated in this system during a mesocosm experiment completed in 2011 (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of nutrient stoichiometry, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During the summer season, Lagunita shrinks substantially and the surface water temperature increases.
source: During the summer season, the pond shrinks substantially and the surface water temperature increases.
evidence: This is a description of seasonal dynamics at the study site.

claim: On 25 May 2012, five replicate enclosures were established in different parts of the pond as unenriched treatments.
source: On 25 May 2012, prior to initiation of fertilization, five replicate enclosures were established in different parts of the pond; these were unenriched treatments that served as reference systems for comparison with the pond after enrichment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Each unenriched mesocosm consisted of a 40 cm diameter clear plastic tube enclosing around 41 L.
source: As in Lee et al. (2015) and Lee et al. (2017), each unenriched mesocosm consisted of a 40 cm diameter clear plastic tube enclosing around 41 L (based on an average depth of 0.33 m at the time at which the mesocosms were installed).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus, with citations to previous work using similar methods.

claim: The mesocosms were fully open to the atmosphere and sediments.
source: The mesocosms were fully open to the atmosphere and sediments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The 41 L volume is a typical size for an aquatic mesocosm.
source: The 41 L volume is a typical size for an aquatic mesocosm (e.g., see review of 350 mesocosms by Petersen et al., 1999)
evidence: This is a statement about methodological standards, supported by citation to Petersen et al., 1999.

claim: The mesocosms encompassed in the order of 30 billion prokaryotic cells.
source: and appropriate for microbial studies, encompassing in the order of 30 billion prokaryotic cells (estimated from our cell counts).
evidence: This is an estimate based on cell count data from the study.

claim: The fertilization procedure was based on a previous mesocosm experiment in Lagunita.
source: The fertilization procedure was based on a previous mesocosm experiment in Lagunita (Lee et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with citations to previous work.

claim: The pond was fertilized to increase the PO43– concentration in the water by 1 μM (as KH2PO4).
source: Based on the pond's volume, we fertilized to increase the PO43– concentration in the water by 1 μM (as KH2PO4).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental treatment.

claim: NH4NO3 was added in a 16:1 (molar) N:P ratio with the added P.
source: We also added NH4NO3 in a 16:1 (molar) N:P ratio with the added P.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental treatment.

claim: The soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) concentration of the pond was measured every 3–4 days.
source: The soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) concentration of the pond was then measured every 3–4 days, after which we added sufficient KH2PO4 to bring the pond's in situ concentration back to 1 μM, along with the appropriate amount of NH4NO3 to achieve a 16:1 molar ratio.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental monitoring protocol.

claim: A sustained whole-ecosystem fertilization treatment was performed, with replicate internal unfertilized mesocosms serving as reference systems.
source: We thus performed a sustained whole-ecosystem fertilization treatment, with replicate internal unfertilized mesocosms serving as reference systems.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental design.

claim: Whole-ecosystem manipulation assures that any experimental responses are ecologically relevant, because the manipulated system encompasses the full scale and scope of ecosystem processes that might modulate that response.
source: Whole-ecosystem manipulation assures that any experimental responses are ecologically relevant, because the manipulated system encompasses the full scale and scope of ecosystem processes that might modulate that response (Carpenter, 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of whole-ecosystem experiments, supported by citation to Carpenter, 1998.

claim: True replication of whole-ecosystem manipulations is very rarely achieved, at least in aquatic ecosystems.
source: Indeed, true replication of whole-ecosystem manipulations is very rarely achieved, at least in aquatic ecosystems.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of whole-ecosystem experiments.

claim: The study followed the recommendations of Carpenter (1989) and Carpenter (1998), relying on the application of a strong experimental treatment at the ecosystem scale together with replication of internal reference mesocosms.
source: We thus followed the recommendations of Carpenter (1989) and Carpenter (1998), relying on the application of a strong experimental treatment at the ecosystem scale and informed by previous experimentation (Lee et al., 2017) together with replication of internal reference mesocosms to assess the impacts of nutrient fertilization.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale, supported by citations to Carpenter, 1989 and Carpenter, 1998.

claim: A whole-ecosystem fertilization of the pond was preferred over fertilizing internal mesocosms within the pond because the smaller enclosures might have provided an artificial view of how the microbial community responds to a nutrient perturbation at the ecosystem scale.
source: We preferred a whole-ecosystem fertilization of the pond over fertilizing internal mesocosms within the pond because the smaller enclosures might have provided an artificial view of how the microbial community responds to a nutrient perturbation at the ecosystem scale.
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental design choice.

claim: Mesocosms cut off many sources of colonizing species (such as shore sediments/soils in ponds) that can contribute to community reorganization following a perturbation.
source: In addition, mesocosms cut off many sources of colonizing species (such as shore sediments/soils in ponds) that can contribute to community reorganization following a perturbation (e.g., Thibault and Brown, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of mesocosm experiments, supported by citation to Thibault and Brown, 2008.

claim: Using internal reference systems rather than other whole ponds avoids introducing confounding factors related to variation between ponds and instead introduces just one potentially confounding factor, the difference in size between the unfertilized mesocosms and the fertilized pond.
source: Given the enormous heterogeneity between communities and water chemistry from different sites within the area, as well as the ability of microbes to disperse between ponds, using internal reference systems rather than other whole ponds is arguably more informative as it avoids introducing confounding factors related to variation between ponds (such as contrasting microbial communities) and instead introduces just one potentially confounding factor, the difference in size between the unfertilized mesocosms and the fertilized pond.
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental design choice.

claim: Following initiation of fertilization, the pond and internal unfertilized mesocosms were sampled every four days to monitor basic biogeochemical and ecological responses.
source: Following initiation of fertilization, the pond and internal unfertilized mesocosms were sampled every four days to monitor basic biogeochemical and ecological responses (see Appendix 1 for water chemistry sampling details).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling protocol.

claim: At the end of the experiment (32 days), five water samples from the pond itself (fertilized treatment) and one water sample from inside each of the five unfertilized internal mesocosms were sampled for metagenomics.
source: At the end of the experiment (32 days), we sampled for metagenomics: five water samples from the pond itself (fertilized treatment) and one water sample from inside each of the five unfertilized internal mesocosms.
evidence: This is a description of the metagenomic sampling design.

claim: Comparing metagenomic data from the pond pre-fertilization to those from the fertilized pond 33 days later would be an inappropriate approach for gaining insight into the effects of fertilization given substantial seasonal changes in temperatures and water chemistry.
source: It is worth noting that, given the substantial seasonal changes in temperatures and water chemistry, we think that comparing metagenomic data from the pond pre-fertilization to those from the fertilized pond 33 days later would be an inappropriate approach for gaining insight into the effects of fertilization.
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental design choice.

claim: Microbes in the water samples were filtered onto sterile GF/F filters (0.7 µm nominal pore size).
source: Microbes in the water samples were filtered onto sterile GF/F filters (0.7 µm nominal pore size, Whatman, Piscataway, NJ, USA)
evidence: This is a description of the sample processing method.

claim: Given the 0.70 µm pore size, extremely small prokaryotes were not part of the metagenomes and so the results do not apply to picobacterioplankton.
source: Given the 0.70 µm pore size, extremely small prokaryotes were not part of our metagenomes and so our results do not apply to these picobacterioplankton.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the sampling method.

claim: If picoplankton were included, they would augment predicted community-level trait responses to fertilization, as picoplankton are slow-growers, tend to do poorly in nutrient-rich waters, have small genomes, and are likely to decrease in abundance in the fertilized treatment.
source: If anything, their inclusion would augment predicted community-level trait responses to fertilization, as picoplankton are slow-growers, tend to do poorly in nutrient-rich waters, have small genomes, and so are likely to decrease in abundance in the fertilized treatment.
evidence: This is speculation about how inclusion of picoplankton would affect results.

claim: Raw reads were trimmed of barcodes, quality filtered, and rarefied to 100,000 sequences per sample.
source: Raw reads were trimmed of barcodes, quality filtered, and rarefied to 100,000 sequences per sample (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the bioinformatic processing methods.

claim: Two samples from the fertilized treatment and one sample from the unfertilized treatment were left out of subsequent analyses because they had sequencing depths less than 20% of the rest of the samples and low-quality scores.
source: Two samples from the fertilized treatment and one sample from the unfertilized treatment were left out of subsequent analyses because they had sequencing depths less than 20% of the rest of the samples (whose sequencing depth averaged 2.5 × 106 reads) and low-quality scores.
evidence: This is a description of data quality control procedures.

claim: Sequences were phylogenetically annotated using the Automated Phylogenetic Inference System (APIS) with default parameters.
source: Sequences were phylogenetically annotated using the Automated Phylogenetic Inference System (APIS) with default parameters, which is designed to optimize annotation accuracy (Zeigler Allen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the bioinformatic analysis method, with citation to the tool.

claim: The program tRNAscan-SE v1.4 was used with the provided general tRNA model to count the number of tRNA genes in non-sub-sampled libraries.
source: The program tRNAscan-SE v1.4 (Lowe and Eddy, 1997), which is specifically designed for recognizing tRNA genes, was used with the provided general tRNA model in order to count the number of tRNA genes in non-sub-sampled libraries.
evidence: This is a description of the bioinformatic analysis method, with citation to the tool.

claim: Variation in the total number of tRNA genes indicates variation in gene copy numbers, as the number of tRNA genes per genome is driven by variation in tRNA gene copy number rather than by tRNA diversity.
source: Variation in the total number of tRNA genes indicates variation in gene copy numbers, as the number of tRNA genes per genome is driven by variation in tRNA gene copy number rather than by tRNA diversity (Higgs and Ran, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of tRNA gene counts, supported by citation to Higgs and Ran, 2008.

claim: The observed rarity of Eukarya and insignificant changes in the groups' relative abundances between treatments indicate that the tRNAscan-SE results reflect variation in prokaryotes, namely Bacteria, rather than in Eukaryotes.
source: Although the tRNAscan-SE approach that we employed did not distinguish between Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes, the observed rarity of Eukarya and insignificant changes in the groups' relative abundances between treatments (see 'Results') indicate that the tRNAscan-SE results, and data from our other bioinformatic analyses, reflect variation in prokaryotes, namely Bacteria (Archaea are very rare in CCB samples; Lee et al., 2017), rather than in Eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the tRNA data based on taxonomic composition results.

claim: Bacterial genome sizes were estimated according to methods in Zeigler Allen et al. (2012).
source: Bacterial genome sizes were estimated according to methods in Zeigler Allen et al. (2012) (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method, with citation to the source.

claim: ENC and ENC′ are relatively statistically well-behaved and insensitive to short gene lengths compared to other measures of codon usage bias.
source: ENC and ENC are relatively statistically well-behaved and insensitive to short gene lengths compared to other measures of codon usage bias (Novembre, 2002; Wright, 1990).
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the codon usage bias metrics, supported by citations to Novembre, 2002 and Wright, 1990.

claim: ENC′ accounts for departures in background nucleotide composition from a uniform distribution and is therefore considered to provide a more powerful and reliable measure of codon usage bias.
source: ENC′ also accounts for departures in background nucleotide composition from a uniform distribution and is therefore considered to provide a more powerful and reliable measure of codon usage bias (Novembre, 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of ENC′, supported by citation to Novembre, 2002.

claim: There are multiple bioinformatic challenges to resolving precisely the phylogenetic composition of entire microbial prokaryotic communities.
source: There are multiple bioinformatic challenges to resolving precisely the phylogenetic composition of entire microbial prokaryotic communities and ensuring that the phylogenetic biases of various molecular methods do not differ between environments or growth conditions (Kunin et al., 2010; Sunagawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about methodological challenges, supported by citations to Kunin et al., 2010 and Sunagawa et al., 2013.

claim: There are massive gaps in prokaryotic taxonomic databases.
source: For instance, there are massive gaps in prokaryotic taxonomic databases (Rinke et al., 2013; Temperton and Giovannoni, 2012)
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in databases, supported by citations to Rinke et al., 2013 and Temperton and Giovannoni, 2012.

claim: Metagenomes generated from low and high growth communities in oceans have different levels of taxonomy blindness.
source: and metagenomes generated from low and high growth communities in oceans have different levels of taxonomy blindness (Kalenitchenko et al., 2018; Sogin et al., 2006; Yooseph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about biases in metagenomic analysis, supported by citations to Kalenitchenko et al., 2018; Sogin et al., 2006; and Yooseph et al., 2010.

claim: DNA sequence assembly introduces a bias, as clonal populations with even low coverage assemble very well whereas high abundance populations with strain diversity will not assemble well.
source: Also, DNA sequence assembly introduces a bias, as clonal populations with even low coverage assemble very well whereas high abundance populations with strain diversity will not assemble well.
evidence: This is a statement about technical biases in metagenomic assembly.
